It would be mere speculation on my part if I tried to describe those soldiers, but those were probably the same young soldiers who had brought us there in the first place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You use the word "jeep." The vehicle that you travelled in, are you able to say if it was a military vehicle or a private vehicle?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a military vehicle. It had no proper seat be side. Along the whole length of the car it had some sort of a tin bench on either side, a one-piece long seat, as it were, along the side of the car.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know any of the soldiers or the names of the soldiers who were accompanying you in the jeep?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not know any of them, but I heard from others, Mr. Cakalic specifically, that he knew the driver, Mile Bakic. And there was another soldier who was sitting at the back with us, apparently his name was Guja, Goran Vuja. I can't remember exactly. But personally, personally I did not know any of them. Nobody mentioned the third soldier who was with us or knew him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were the soldiers armed or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did the jeep go to, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The jeep returned us to Vukovar as they'd probably been ordered to do, to drive us back to Velepromet. However, once we reached the gate of Velepromet, there was a uniformed person waiting for us there who was probably in charge of letting people in and out through the main gate where the administration building is. This person told the driver that there was no room for us inside and that he should take us to a private company called Modateks about two or three kilometres from Velepromet if you drive back down the main road, if you drive south.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to deal with the people who were inside that vehicle. You gave us the name of individuals who were in a group outside the Ovcara hangar. Did any of these people travel in that vehicle to Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, all of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us then deal, please, with when you arrived at Velepromet. What occurred?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing. We remained seated inside the vehicles. The soldier came up to the driver and told him what I've just told you, that he should take us to Modateks, the private company.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you go to Modateks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did. We were received there by an elderly gentleman with a white beard who was wearing a uniform. They called him grand-dad. He was probably in charge in one way or another of what was going on inside this hall of this company. He took us aside and sat us down at a long table about one metre across and two metres long. We were some sort of a separate group at that table. Inside this hall belonging to this company when we came we found a large number of civilians there. Nearly 100 per cent women and children. We were separated from those, and we were at this table, and this is also where we spent the night. We were guarded by young armed soldiers. We stayed there until about 1400 hours the next day when this gentleman came along. His last name was Kusic [phoen], the one they called grand-dad, and he told us they would have to drive us back to Velepromet. At this point he, Jezdimir Stankovic and a third person I did not know, all armed, walked us back to Velepromet. Once we arrived in Velepromet, we crossed the entire yard and reached a room they refer to as the joiner's room.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just want to deal with one of the names that you have mentioned, and that is a gentleman called Stankovic. Had you seen Stankovic before?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is the same Jezdimir Stankovic --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where did you --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031 [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- that I had seen at the barracks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. When you were taken to Velepromet, where were you placed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were placed in this room that they called the joiner's room or the carpenter's room.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware of a name or nickname that it was given subsequently?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Later on, I realised that this room had been nicknamed the death room.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were taken to this room, how many soldiers escorted you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The three soldiers who were escorting us on our way from Modateks, until they handed us over once we had reached that room.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anything happen to you prior to going into the room itself?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Outside the room there is a broad corridor. We were received there by two soldiers. One of them was sitting on some sort of a chair and the other soldier searched us. This soldier took the last of my money, the little money that I still had on me. He told me to take off my watch, too. I was made to stand outside the door with my hands against the wall. He realised that I was wearing a wrist-watch. He told me to take it off, which I did, but as he was talking to the other soldier, I closed my watch with my fist in toward conceal it so he probably didn't remember to ask for it again. I kept the watch throughout, and I still had it when I returned to Croatia eventually.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to deal with the room itself. When you went into the room, were there any other people inside the room?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were people there. The place was full. People were standing or lying on -- on dirty blankets, muddy blankets. There might have been between 25 and 30 people altogether in that room.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what were the conditions like inside the room itself?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031 [Resumed]
utterances.text: People were crest-fallen. There was hardly anybody who was talking to anybody else. Those who were talking kept their voices very low. Those were probably people who were close, who knew each other. But there was no proper conversation taking place, and nobody was really moving much at all, those prisoners, if I may call them that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have told us about the group of people who were held outside the Ovcara hangar, that that group of people had been taken to Modateks. When you came to the Velepromet facility, how many of that group remained together and were placed inside the room?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031 [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we're talking about that group, the people who were arrested at the hospital and brought over to Ovcara from the barracks and the hospital and then driven back to Modateks, there was six of us there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the young boy Tomas Baumgertner. Was he taken to the Velepromet facility?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. When I was leaving, he was still sitting on the ground to the left of the hangar entrance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am sorry, we better just clarify, because I thought I had asked you whether that group had travelled into Vukovar. Perhaps the best way of dealing with it is of the people who were in the group outside the hangar, who remained outside the hangar and who went to Vukovar? Can you help us with that? Who was left and who went to Vukovar with you?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I must object to this. I think this is a leading question, because when the witness first spoke about this he described a group of seven people. He gave us all their names one by one and said that they were in the van. Now the Prosecutor is trying to lead the witness on who stayed behind and who was off. I believe this is a leading question on the part of the OTP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I understand what is happening quite differently from you, Mr. Lukic. I think there is a -- some lack of certainty or clarity about whether the group of soldiers by the hangar door at Ovcara to which the young 17-year-old joined is the same group that was moved later into Velepromet and so forth in the jeep. And I think you have one quite clear understanding, Mr. Moore has perhaps another, and I am confused in the middle, and there may be others in a similar position. So I think a little time by Mr. Moore in a non-leading way, as he is doing, will help clarify it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, can you just try and help us? I know it's difficult. When you left the group of people by the Ovcara hangar, how many people were left and how many people went in the vehicle to Vukovar? Are you able to tell us?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Your question assumes something, Mr. Moore, which may not be valid, as to who the group is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: The witness gave the name of the group of people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That was a group outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I don't think it was a group that included the lad Baumgertner.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: My recollection is it did include Baumgertner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Maybe that's where the confusion is, and you're assuming by your question there is but one group.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I will -- I will try and clarify again. I have no problems about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, the group who were outside the Ovcara hangar, do you remember the group that you joined? And you told us their names. How many of that group went to Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Seven persons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And are you able to tell us the names of the people who travelled in the jeep to Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Emil Cakalic, Dragutin Berghofer, Tihomir Perkovic, Vladimir Dudas, Zarko Kojic, and a soldier I didn't know and I did not know his name at the time. Six plus one equals seven.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And of that group how many eventually went to the Velepromet room?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Six persons from that group went to Velepromet while we were at Modateks, some soldiers came to get Zarko Kojic. They took him away to his grandmother's place. That's where they told him they would be taking him. So he was taken away from Modateks to a private home in Vukovar. The rest of us six persons altogether were taken back to Velepromet and left in what they refer to as the joiner's room.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you stay in that room? Are you able to estimate?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We arrived there between 2.00 and 3.00 p.m. We walked there slowly, and we stayed in the room for the whole evening and until late at night, between 11.00 and 11.30 p.m.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were in the room at Velepromet, the people who were in there, did they remain in there or were any removed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The room was locked. The soldier who was there when we arrived and who searched us and took us into the room would sporadically allow certain paramilitaries into the room. These paramilitaries who came into the room would pick prisoners for themselves and take them away. That was how Karlo Crk was removed. That was how Krunoslav Golac was removed. And that was how a third person was removed, Tihomir Perkovic. These three persons did not return to that room for as long as we were there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you seen --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you seen Perkovic since that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you seen Karlo Crk since that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what about the third person, Golac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. Never again. They're gone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we deal then, please, with the leaving of Velepromet itself? When did you leave Velepromet approximately?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometime at night, between 11.00 and 11.30 p.m. A JNA captain walked into the room who said that we should all get ready and that he would take us over to the barracks because there was a danger that we might all die in that room over the night. We obeyed, and we all left. We were being escorted by JNA soldiers. They took us to an area inside the -- in the yard, and we were boarded onto buses in the presence of this captain and the soldiers escorting us. We were driven to the Vukovar barracks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to just clarify the arrival of the JNA captain taking you to the JNA barracks. Did you have a conversation with him at that time or did he say anything to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have a conversation with him. There was no chance. Some of the soldiers perhaps did. He probably gave them some sort of a reason, but the reason I knew and I was told is there was a risk that we would come in harm's way during the night, and he said this was the reason he was taking us to the barracks. That's what I know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You go to the barracks and approximately how long do you stay there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We stay there for one night or half a night, until the next morning, 8.00. At 8.00 the next morning, one of the soldiers came. He put our names down on a list. He called out our names. There were 38 of us. We were put onto a bus and driven to Sremska Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to deal with the 38 people you say approximately were in that JNA barracks. Do you know where those 38 persons had come from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They all came from the death room, or the joiner's room, and yet another room that was a little further off from the joiner's room.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I deal, then, with the removal of most people from the joiner's room? When those people were removed from that room, were there any people left in the joiner's room? Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. I left, and I don't know whether somebody stayed back. All I know is that those of us who came in two buses, I don't know how many there were there, but I know that some of those remained in the barracks, in the room where we were, whereas 38 of us, our names were put down on a list and then we were taken to the prison in Sremska Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just want to clarify one piece of your evidence. You've told us you were taken to a room at the JNA barracks and there were a number of people there. You then have mentioned the figure 38 that were listed and subsequently removed. Were any people left after the 38 were removed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Some remained, some of those who were in the same room in the barracks. I don't know how many remained. 38 of us were boarded on the buses, those that had come from Velepromet. I don't know how many remain. There was a woman among them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of the people that remain, you've said that there was a woman amongst them. I'm not trying to lead, if there is any objection to the way I put the question. I will put it then in the following way: Does that suggest that the rest were male who were left or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the males plus the one woman who were left, did you know any of them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did. After five days, a group was brought in, some of my acquaintances who had been brought in from Velepromet to the barracks, and they were later brought to Sremska Mitrovica. In the room where I was in Sremska Mitrovica, five of such persons arrived there. I never asked whether everybody from the barracks had been brought in and then placed in separate rooms or perhaps only some of them were brought to Sremska Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Would Your Honour give me one moment. I wish to clarify one matter. I have no further questions. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Moore. Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Cross-examined by Mr. Vasic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good evening to everybody in the courtroom. Good evening, Witness. First of all I'd like to introduce myself. I'm Miroslav Vasic, attorney-at-law, one of the Defence counsel of Mr. Mrksic. Before I start with my cross-examination, I would like to ask you something. Since both of us speak the same language, would you please make a pause before answering my questions so that the interpreters have enough time to correctly interpret everything that we're saying. There is also another reason for this, so that your voice doesn't leak, so to speak, through my microphone and so that your identity remains fully protected. First of all, I would like to clarify some technical details concerning the statements that you gave and that my learned friend from the Prosecution covered with you yesterday. You said that at one point in time on the 27th of July, you gave a statement in Zagreb, and I would like to know to whom. I suppose you know which statement I'm referring to.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I said that. And I also said that I simply didn't know to whom I gave this statement. I simply don't remember that, and I don't know how this Tribunal obtained that statement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you give any statements in 1992 to the organs of the Ministry of the Interior of Croatia or to any other state institutions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't give any written statements. However, there were certain interviews. I would receive a notice from certain organs to appear for an interview, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the statement from July of 1992? Did it ensue as a result of such interviews?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you that I simply didn't remember. I can't connect the two. I know that this is what is stated on that statement, but I can't remember. And I myself would like to know this if possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you kindly for your answer. In this statement that gave in 1995, the one that you didn't sign, the one that you gave to the Prosecutor, you said that this interview took place in Budapest. Could you please tell us who you talked with there, and did you give any statements there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The two of us who were Ovcara survivors travelled there. We went there as witnesses to give our statement at a meeting organised by a commission of the government of Croatia, commission for missing persons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, please, were there any representatives of the Yugoslav army at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And I omitted to mention this, namely I did not give any written statements there. There was just an interview held. Now, as to whether somebody compiled the statement based on the interview, I don't know about that. The representatives of the Yugoslav army were there. I think that there was a colonel there. His last name was Starcevic, and then there was Dr. Stankovic, a pathologist there, and then another gentleman was there. I don't know whether he was a military person or not. He wore civilian clothes, and his last name was Korac. He was a representative of the Red Cross of the then Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you for this exhaustive answer. Tell me, please, do you remember whether this meeting was held in July of 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was. If I'm not mistaken, it was on the 29th of July in 1992 or perhaps 1993. I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to ask you once again to make a pause before answering my questions. I want to make sure that your voice is not heard through my microphone. When asked by my learned friend, you said that you had two meetings with the OTP, once in 1995, once in 1996. After your first interview, you did not sign your statement, but you signed it after the second interview. I would like to know whether you gave both of this -- of these statements to the best of your recollection at the time.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first statement is something that I wouldn't assign much value to. I gave it at the request of an investigator of this Tribunal. When I said that I wasn't prepared to give a statement that I would later sign and that I wasn't prepared to come and testify here, he asked me to at least come and meet and talk to him so that he would gain a picture, an information about what had happened in the Vukovar Hospital. This is how this statement was compiled, based on this discussion that we had. It was a bit more loose, and I don't know if it can be treated as a proper statement, because of course I did not give my consent. And it wasn't until just a few months ago that I learned that the statement had been compiled and sent to the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Can you please clarify for us why did you refuse at that time to give a statement that you would sign and to come and testify here before this Court?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031 [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I had very serious health problems at the time, which came as a result of the three months of living in Vukovar under war conditions and then three months spent in the camp in Sremska Mitrovica. If you add then experiences at the Vukovar Hospital, the barracks, and the Ovcara, then you get the idea. And I didn't want to subject myself to further trouble and strain. Therefore, I didn't want to give a statement that I would sign, and I didn't want to come and testify here, precisely because of these reasons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you explained your position to the investigator, did you tell him that you were not satisfied in the way that European Commission was investigating the events in Ovcara and that that was one of the reasons why you refused to give a statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I said so. In those days, we saw on television and we read in the papers about a statement given by the UN representative who was investigating war crimes. This person gave a statement expressing doubts and expressing reservation about our views and our statements, even though we did our best to be sincere and as clear as possible when giving statements. I thought that he, as a representative of a very prominent international organisation, had a -- an inaccurate picture of our of our plight and suffering. This hurt me, and this is why I said that I wasn't ready to testify and give a statement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. After this, in 1996, you consented to meet with the investigator to give a statement and to come here to testify. However, when they contacted you in 1998, once again you refused to come and testify. You wrote an addendum with an investigator to your statement that you signed. It was done at that time; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the reason you gave to the investigator for refusing to come to the Tribunal and testify in the proceedings against Slavko Dokmanovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031 [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of the reasons was the one I gave you in my previous answer, namely my health. The second reason I refused to testify against the late Slavko Dokmanovic was that I persistently claimed in all of my statements, later on I had to correct it because there were some things that were not clear, is that I did not see, did not recognise Mr. Dokmanovic at Ovcara. Other people told me that he was there, and when talked to the investigator I mentioned his name saying that he was also there. I heard this from two witnesses who confirmed in writing seeing him there. They signed their statements. But I thought that it wasn't ethical of me. It wasn't proper of me to testify against him when I learned of his presence there from other people. Mr. Dokmanovic was accused of serious crimes, and this is why I refused to testify against him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us that you had to correct some of your statements. Can you please tell us how this came about that you had to make amendments and corrections?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This pertained to this third statement that I signed. My statement mentioned that Mr. Dokmanovic was seen at Ovcara, and I had to add to that that this is something that I had learned from others who had seen him there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember now when you gave this third statement? Do you remember what year and what month?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031 [Resumed]
utterances.text: 1996. The 25th and 26th of April.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I understand this correctly, this is your second statement, the one you gave after 1995, not your third statement.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Nevertheless, after your second statement, you wrote an addendum explaining your reasons for refusing to testify in that case. You said that you signed this. Would you agree with me that nowhere in that particular amendment or addendum did you indicate this reason, the reason being that you were no eye-witness to this, no first-hand witness. The only reasons you gave at the time were your health and your personal safety. Would that seem to be accurate?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's accurate. That's precisely what it says. I wrote that and, as I have already said, I did not realise at the time that a statement had been drawn up or its substance. I did not know that the investigator had not in fact listed this as one of my reasons. I didn't know at the time. I don't know it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: With the utmost respect, my learned friend unintentionally may be misleading the Court and the witness, because if I just draw his attention to the statements of the 25th and 26th of April of 1996, at page 00280, there is reference to something that the witness specifically wanted to mention. May I just -- just locate it? It starts: "As regards Dokmanovic, there is something to say." With the utmost respect, in fairness to the witness, the totality must go in because he's now being asked the reason why he didn't say something, but in actual fact in the statement it does say that he specifically wanted to exclude the matter in relation to Dokmanovic. It's not a case of merely saying Dokmanovic did this or Dokmanovic did that. He is categorically saying and excluding Dokmanovic from the issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I tend not to agree with my learned friend. I think this statement mentioned here dated the 25th and 26th of April is not exclusive. However, I'm not talking about that statement. I'm talking about the addendum made following the 1998 statement explaining one thing and one thing alone, why he refuses to appear before this Court as a witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The one thing. There are two things, health and personal safety.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely, Your Honour. Thank you very much. I just wanted to try to clarify this with the witness, which would hopefully provide a complete answer to a question asked by my colleague yesterday receiving merely a partial answer in relation to reasons having to do with the witness's possible presence and any observations that he may have made about Slavko Dokmanovic. Thank you very much. I would like to move into private session, if possible, please. I have some --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that after the 2nd of May, 1991, a Crisis Staff was established in the Vukovar Medical Centre at the order of the government of the Republic of Croatia, rather, the Ministry of Health?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that there was an organ which, how shall I put it, was in charge of the hospital and its operation. Now, who appointed this organ and precisely what was its task, I wouldn't know because I was not a member of this organ.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The work obligation regime, did it also entail after the 2nd of May putting the hospital on the alert of second degree in order to prepare it to take in the wounded?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After the events of the 2nd of May, 1991, do you know whether the doctors and other medical personnel of Serb ethnicity stopped coming to work?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there also a decrease in the number of Serb patients coming to seek assistance at the medical centre?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I doesn't know. This is a question for a medical staff member.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you present in the hospital building on the 2nd of May, 1991?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to say now. I simply don't know. It's been a long time. You're asking me about a specific date. No, I wouldn't be able to answer that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm asking you this because on that day the casualties from Borovo Selo were brought in, the wounded and those who were killed. Therefore, I'm asking you whether you saw them arriving in the hospital, and I'm also asking you whether you heard that after this they were guarded by the armed members of the Croatian MUP.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, once again I have to tell you that (redacted)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both. Those who were medical personnel, by virtue of their profession and the oath that they took, had to work even longer hours, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you at some pointed after May of 1991, together with the other residents of your building, organise some kind of a watch shift or some kind of a defence?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There was no need for that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us when was this organised?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was an internal arrangement among some individuals who received their instructions from I don't know whom to see if a group of tenants could be organised in apartment buildings, there were 18 or 19 buildings in that neighbourhood, in order to assist the elderly and the infirm to find food, to ensure that they had all the supplies, enough water and medical assistance, if needed. This is how we organised ourselves within our building. I, who was employed at the time, could only do this outside of work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You didn't tell us when was this arrangement put in place.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Later on, in October or so. It did not exist during the summer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear that in certain streets in Vukovar after May of 1991, residents organised defence groups to defend themselves from the local Serb residents and that this was organised by the Croatian Democratic Union?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031 [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, this allegation of yours is quite harsh and aimed against one ethnicity. I did not hear anything of this nature. I never heard that such groups were organised in any part of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that in spring of 1991 the management level personnel of Serb ethnicity was removed from office in a lot of companies in Vukovar and that in the medical centre where you were employed this happened a bit later? Do you know about this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I wasn't interested in that. I don't know reasons for this, nor do I know persons who were removed from offices at the time. I was not a prominent leader or a politician, and there was no way I could learn about this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your statement, you said that you knew Mr. Dokmanovic. Do you know that after the first multi-party elections he was elected president of the Vukovar Municipal Assembly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us how long was he able to perform his duties, and also, if you know, when was the Assembly of Vukovar municipality disbanded pursuant to the government orders, and when was government's commissioner appointed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that, and I hesitate to speak of Mr. Dokmanovic. He is dead, and as you know, it is not proper to speak ill of the dead. I know that he was president of the Vukovar Municipal Assembly, and then he was removed from office and the commissioner was appointed.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters didn't hear the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I didn't know that. I could not learn of this. I was unable to obtain such information.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that in June and July 1991 explosives were placed in certain houses in Vukovar and also in Borba newsstand in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard this either from the press or from my friends and acquaintances. Based on what I heard, this happened on both sides. The Borba newsstand that you asked about, I don't know for a fact that it was blown up. I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, we have run well over the time that we were allowing for a session with the present witness, and I think it might be in the interests of us all if we wound up for the day now and to resume tomorrow morning at 9.00. We will be adjourning now for the evening, and your evidence will continue tomorrow at 9.00 in the morning. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
